correctness.rationale: With prescribed column sup norms, the objective is convex on the box of matrix entries and some box vertex maximizes it. Each vertex has the prescribed norms, including zero weights. A projective sign class with a represented row attains T²; an absent class differs from any row and its negative, so both agreement and disagreement have weight at least b, giving a bound (T−2b)². There are at most m represented classes. Flipping one coordinate of minimum weight pairs the classes without fixed points for n≥2; deleting one from each of r≤k/2 different pairs realizes the bound in every class. At fixed squared sum and minimum b the objective increases with T, so making the remaining n−1 norms equal is optimal by Cauchy–Schwarz. For d=n−1 the quotient then is (d²+dAq+q²)/(d+q²) with q∈[0,1]. The top eigenvector of the displayed symmetric matrix is feasible: for d>1 its q equals dA/[2(λ₊−1)]≤1; squaring if needed reduces the inequality to d(d−1)A(2−A)≥0. For d=1, q=1 suffices when A>0 and all ratios work at A=0. This gives both endpoints, including n=2,m=1 and m=k. The five-row witness has three absent classes paired by column 3 and q=√19−4; substitution gives 2+√19/4.
residual_risks: The replay is a small-domain diagnostic; the uniform upper bound, pairing and Rayleigh argument establish the theorem for all stated integers. The formula is real and does not extend here to smaller m or the modified unit-sphere constant.

evidence: The preprint gives the general sign operator and proves saturation at every m≥2^{n−1} via sign rows. The Rademacher lemma concerns p>2 in L_p/ℓ_p, not the fixed-norm optimum in the finite real cube. The 1998 repository item did not yield its full original text.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The saturated construction uses all classes. It does not imply sharp coverage when some classes must be absent. An inaccessible foundational paper creates an explicit residual risk, not evidence against the distinct result.

evidence: The three-class argument already gives [3T²+(T−2b)²]/4 when n=m=3, and its optimization yields the same upper constant. The primary saturation proof covers r=0. For r>1 in general the prior all-row or one-deletion constructions do not establish simultaneous sharp coverage of all missing classes; the pairing along a minimum-weight coordinate does.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Neither the full-sign endpoint nor the earlier four-class case dominates the weighted formula for arbitrarily many deletions up to k/2. The shared sign-row structure alone is not a proof of the new optimum.

evidence: The same unrestricted real objective is the squared norm of the all-sign operator T_n divided by 2^{n−1}; it is also the squared Rademacher sign-average on the coordinate cube. This equivalence does not identify it with the modified objective at t_j=1, or with a geometric product of signed norms.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The operator/Rademacher representations bring the same object into scope. The modified or geometric objectives change the norm optimization or aggregation and are not equivalent.

checked_sources: Frozen fixed-length theorem and exact five-row example; independent exact reproduction; prior saturation and n=m=3 checks
value.rationale: The result supplies exact values of a standard Banach-space geometric invariant where the dimension alone no longer guarantees saturation. More strongly it determines worst-case behavior at arbitrary prescribed lengths by a sharp covering construction and identifies a genuinely intermediate value at n=4,m=5. The weighted construction explains why optimizing at unequal lengths can matter.
residual_risks: Does not solve the more sparse code-covering regime, and makes no claim for complex scalars or the modified constant.
